Game over! And interestingly: "executed actions: UP, LEFT, LEFT, UP" — only 4 actions were executed before game over (not all 8). And the reds are at (24,24), (30,30), (36,12) — wait, the red that was at (24,30) is now at (30,30)! The red moved from (24,30) to (30,30)!
Let me reconstruct: my batch was UP, LEFT, LEFT, UP, LEFT, LEFT, LEFT, DOWN. Only the first 4 were executed: UP, LEFT, LEFT, UP.
- Start (42,42).
- UP → (36,42)
- LEFT → (36,36)
- LEFT → (36,30)
- UP → (30,30)
And then game over. Why? The red at (24,30) moved to (30,30) — the cell where the player moved! The red moved down from (24,30) to (30,30) — vertically, 6 cells, onto the player!
So in level 3, the reds can strike vertically too! Or: the reds strike when the player is 6 cells away in a straight line (horizontal or vertical). In level 2, the player was at (33,36), 6 below the red — the red didn't strike. Hmm, this contradicts.
Wait, let me re-verify level 2: player at (33,36), red at (27,36). 6 apart vertically. The red didn't move. Then the player moved UP onto the red and captured it. So in level 2, vertical proximity was safe.
In level 3: player moved UP from (36,30) to (30,30). The red at (24,30) is 6 above (30,30). The red moved down onto the player → death.
The difference: in level 2, the player was already at (33,36) (6 below the red) — the red didn't strike while the player was sitting there. In level 3, the player moved to (30,30) — the red struck.
Hmm, so the red strikes when the player moves to a cell 6 away in a straight line (in any direction)? In level 2: the player moved RIGHT from (33,30) to (33,36) — the destination (33,36) is 6 below the red (27,36). The red didn't strike. Contradiction again!
Unless… the red's strike depends on the direction of the player's move: the red strikes when the player moves toward the red (closing the straight-line distance). Level 2: player (33,30)→(33,36) RIGHT: the red is at (27,36) — not in a straight line with the move (the red is up-right, diagonal). Distance from the red to the player: before the move (33,30): diagonal (6,6); after the move (33,36): 6 (vertical). The move closed the distance from 8.5 to 6. Hmm, that's "moving toward" in the Euclidean sense.
Level 3: player (36,30)→(30,30) UP: the red is at (24,30), directly above. The move closed the distance from 12 to 6. The red struck.
Level 2's death: player (27,24)→(27,30) RIGHT: the red is at (27,36), directly to the right. Closed from 12 to 6. The red struck. ✓
Level 2's safe: (33,30)→(33,36) RIGHT: the red is at (27,36). Before: (33,30) to (27,36): Δ(6,6), Euclidean 8.49. After: (33,36) to (27,36): 6. Closed from 8.49 to 6. By this rule the red should have struck. It didn't. ✗
Hmm. So what distinguishes (33,30)→(33,36) [safe] from (36,30)→(30,30) [death]?
- In the safe case, the player's destination is 6 from the red, but the player's move was not along the line connecting the player and the red (the red was diagonal, the move was horizontal).
- In the death case, the player's move was along the line connecting the player and the red (the red was directly above, the move was up).
So the rule: the red strikes when the player moves directly toward the red (the destination is on the line segment between the player and the red, i.e., the player moves along the straight line toward the red, closing to 6 or less).
Equivalently: the red strikes when the player moves in the direction of the red and the post-move straight-line distance is 6 (one hop).
Level 2's death: the player moved RIGHT, the red was to the RIGHT, post-move distance 6 → strike. ✓
Level 2's safe: the player moved RIGHT, the red was up-right (diagonal) → not directly toward → safe. ✓
Level 3's death: the player moved UP, the red was UP, post-move distance 6 → strike. ✓
Level 2's capture: the player moved UP from (33,36) to (27,36): the red was directly above, post-move distance 0 (on top of the red) → capture, not strike. So when the player moves directly toward the red and lands on the red → capture (the red is removed). When the player moves directly toward the red and lands 6 away → the red strikes (moves onto the player) → death.
Interesting! So the red's "attack range" is exactly one hop: if the player moves toward the red and ends up exactly one hop away, the red hops onto the player. If the player moves onto the red, the red is captured (defeated).
Hmm wait, but that means capture is always possible: just keep moving toward the red until you land on it. But the red strikes when you're one hop away… so how do you get onto the red? You'd have to move from one hop away onto the red — but the red strikes when you're one hop away (after your move). Unless the strike only happens when you move toward the red (closing), and moving from one-hop away onto the red is also closing…
Level 2: the player was at (33,36) (one hop below the red). Then moved UP onto the red → capture, no strike. So the red doesn't strike when the player is already one hop away and moves onto the red. The strike only triggers when the player's move ends at exactly one hop (not on top of the red).
So the mechanic: after the player moves, if the player is exactly one hop (6 cells) from the red in a straight line, the red hops onto the player (death). If the player is on top of the red, the red is captured.
Wait, but then in level 2, when the player was at (33,36) (one hop from the red), why didn't the red strike immediately? The player had just moved RIGHT into (33,36). Hmm — the strike rule: the player's move ends one hop from the red in a straight line → strike. (33,36) is one hop below (27,36) — in a straight line (vertical). By this rule the red should have struck. It didn't!
Argh. Let me tabulate all the evidence:
E1 (level 2): player (33,30)→(33,36) RIGHT. Red (27,36) is one hop above the destination. Result: safe.
E2 (level 2): player (33,36)→(27,36) UP. Red was on top of the destination. Result: capture (red removed).
E3 (level 2): player (27,24)→(27,30) RIGHT. Red (27,36) is one hop to the right of the destination. Result: the red moved to (27,30), the player died.
E4 (level 3): player (36,30)→(30,30) UP. Red (24,30) is one hop above the destination. Result: the red moved to (30,30), the player died.
E1 vs E4: both end one hop from the red in a straight line. E1 safe (red above, vertical), E4 death (red above, vertical)!! The geometry is identical! The only difference: in E1 the red was at (27,36) and the destination was (33,36) — the red is above the destination. In E4 the red is at (24,30), the destination is (30,30) — the red is above the destination. Identical!
So why is E1 safe and E4 death??
Difference: the player's move direction relative to the red's position. E1: the player moved RIGHT (horizontal), the red is vertically above the destination. E4: the player moved UP (vertical), the red is vertically above the destination — the move is along the red's line, toward the red.
So the rule: the red strikes when the player moves directly toward the red (the destination is between the player's origin and the red, collinear) and ends up one hop away. E1: the move was not toward the red (the red was off the line of the move) → safe. E3: the move was toward the red → strike. E4: the move was toward the red → strike. E2: the move was toward the red and landed on the red → capture.
This is consistent with all the evidence!
Rule: after the player's move, if the player is collinear with the red and the player moved toward the red: if the player is on top of the red → capture; if the player is exactly one hop (6 cells) from the red → the red hops onto the player (death).
Hmm, or more simply: the red strikes when the player moves toward it and the post-move distance is 6 or less? E2: post-move distance 0 → capture (not death). So: distance 0 → capture; distance 6 (and moved toward) → death.
What if the post-move distance is 12 and the player moved toward the red? In level 2, the player moved (27,18)→(27,24), the red was at (27,36): moved toward, post-move distance 12. No strike. So the strike requires post-move distance exactly 6 (one hop).
OK, so the refined rule: the red hops onto the player when the player's move is directly toward the red and ends exactly one hop away. Moving onto the red = capture (the red is removed).
Now, level 3's board. Reds: (24,24), (24,30), (36,12). Wait — the reds are now at (24,24), (30,30), (36,12)? The post-death frame shows red blocks at (24,24), (30,30), (36,12). The red that was at (24,30) moved to (30,30) (where the player died). After the reset (the level restarts), the reds go back to (24,24), (24,30), (36,12). The current frame is the game-over frame (the level hasn't been reset yet — "still on the same level", state GAME_OVER). Last time, after game over, the next action triggered a reset. Let me check the current frame: is the player visible? Blue: None — the player is gone. The board shows the red at (30,30) (having moved). So this is the death frame.
On the next action, the level will probably reset (as before: after game over, the next action started a fresh level 2… actually, last time after game over, the frame already showed the reset level when I took the next action).
Now, plan level 3 with the refined rule. The danger is moving directly toward a red and ending one hop away.
My path: (42,42) UP (36,42) LEFT (36,36) LEFT (36,30) UP (30,30) ← died here: moving UP toward red (24,30), ending one hop away.
Fix: don't move directly toward a red and end one hop away. Options:
(a) Capture the red: keep moving toward it until you land on it. From (36,30), UP → (30,30) is one hop from red (24,30) → death. So you can't capture (24,30) from below… unless you approach from a different angle. To capture red (24,30), you'd have to land on (24,30) from an adjacent cell: (24,24) [red], (24,36) [white], (18,30) [white], (30,30) [white]. From (24,36): move LEFT toward the red, land on the red → capture! Is (24,36) reachable? (24,36) is connected to (18,36) [g(21,36)], (24,42) [g(24,39)], (24,30 red) [g(24,33)]. And (18,36) ← (18,30) ← (18,24). How to reach row 18? From (30,36)? No, no vertical bridge at column 36 between rows 24 and 30… g(27,36)? No — the black wall B(27,33-47) blocks that region. Hmm: the vertical bridges to row 24 are: g(21,24) [(18,24)-(24,24 red)], g(21,30) [(18,30)-(24,30 red)], g(21,36) [(18,36)-(24,36)], g(27,30) [(24,30 red)-(30,30)], g(27,48) [(24,48)-(30,48)].
So (24,36) is reachable from (18,36) or (24,42). (24,42) from (24,48). (24,48) from (30,48) [g(27,48)]. (30,48) from the row-30 chain.
So: (42,42) UP (36,42) UP? No — (36,42)→(30,42) [g(33,42)] UP → (30,42) → RIGHT (30,48) [g(30,45)] → UP (24,48) [g(27,48)] → LEFT (24,42) [g(24,45)] → LEFT (24,36) [g(24,39)] → LEFT onto red (24,30) [g(24,33)] = capture!
Check each move for "moving directly toward a red and ending one hop away":
- (42,42)→(36,42) UP: reds are (24,24), (24,30), (36,12). (36,42): red (36,12) is in the same row band 36, 30 to the left — not one hop. The move UP is not toward any red. Safe.
- (36,42)→(30,42) UP: red (24,30)? Not collinear with (36,42)→(30,42) (column 42 vs 30). Safe.
- (30,42)→(30,48) RIGHT: red (24,30) is up-left, not on the line. Safe.
- (30,48)→(24,48) UP: reds are in columns 24, 30, 12 — not column 48. Safe.
- (24,48)→(24,42) LEFT: red (24,30) is to the left, 12 away. Moving toward the red! Post-move distance: (24,42) to (24,30) = 12. Not one hop. Safe (the strike requires exactly one hop).
- (24,42)→(24,36) LEFT: red (24,30) is 6 to the left — one hop! Moving toward the red, ending one hop away → the red strikes → death!!
Damn. So (24,36) is a death cell (approaching red (24,30) from the right).
Alternative: capture red (24,30) from above: from (18,30) move DOWN onto (24,30). (18,30) is reachable from (18,24) [g(18,27)] or (18,36) [g(18,33)]. (18,36) from (24,36) — death cell. (18,24) from (18,30) or (24,24 red). (24,24) is a red — capture it first? To capture red (24,24): from (24,30) [red] — no; from (18,24) DOWN: (18,24)→(24,24): moving DOWN toward red (24,24), landing on top of it → capture! Is (18,24) reachable? (18,24)'s connections: (18,30) [g(18,27)], (24,24 red) [g(21,24)]. So (18,24) is only reachable via (18,30) or the red. (18,30) via (18,36) or (24,30 red) [g(21,30)]. (18,36) via (24,36). So the row-18 cluster {(18,24),(18,30),(18,36)} is only reachable via (24,36) [death cell] or the reds. Dead end.
So red (24,30) can't be captured (all approaches: from the right (24,36) = death; from below (30,30) = death; from above (18,30) = unreachable; from the left (24,24) = red).
Red (24,24): approaches: from the right (24,30) = red; from below (30,24): move UP onto (24,24) — moving toward the red, landing on top → capture! Is (30,24) reachable? Yes, via the row-30 chain. But wait — (30,24) is one hop below (24,24). Moving UP from (30,24) to (24,24): the destination is the red → capture (per E2, landing on the red = capture, no strike). But wait — is (30,24) itself a death cell? Standing at (30,24), the red is one hop above. Per E1, standing one hop away is safe as long as you didn't move directly toward the red to get there. How do I get to (30,24)? From (30,30) LEFT: the move is horizontal, the red (24,24) is up-left — not on the line of the move → safe (E1 pattern). Or from (30,18) RIGHT: moving toward red (24,24)? The red is up-right, not on the horizontal line → safe.
So: ...(30,30) → LEFT → (30,24) [safe, E1 pattern] → UP → (24,24) [capture red (24,24)]!
Then, with red (24,24) gone, can I capture red (24,30)? From (24,24) move RIGHT onto (24,30): moving toward the red, landing on top → capture!
Then the row-24 chain is clear: (24,30) → RIGHT → (24,36) [now safe] → RIGHT → (24,42) → RIGHT → (24,48) → DOWN → (30,48)… but wait, I need to get to the target (42,24). Let me replan the whole route.
Goal: reach N(42,24). The target is at (42,24), connected to (42,18) [g(42,21)]. (42,18) from (36,18) [g(39,18)]. (36,18) from (36,12 red) [g(36,15)] or (30,18) [g(33,18)].
Red (36,12): capture from above: (30,12) → DOWN → (36,12): moving toward the red, landing on top → capture. (30,12) from (30,18) LEFT: the move is horizontal, red (36,12) is down-left — not on the line → safe.
So the full plan:
Start (42,42).
1. UP → (36,42) [g(39,42)]
2. UP → (30,42) [g(33,42)]
3. LEFT → (30,36) [g(30,39)]
4. LEFT → (30,30) [g(30,33)] — check: moving LEFT, red (24,30) is above (30,30) — not on the line of the move (the move is horizontal) → safe (E1 pattern).
5. LEFT → (30,24) [g(30,27)] — moving LEFT, red (24,24) is above the destination — not on the line → safe.
6. UP → (24,24) [g(21,24)] — moving UP toward red (24,24), landing on top → capture.
7. RIGHT → (24,30) [g(24,27)] — moving RIGHT toward red (24,30), landing on top → capture.
8. RIGHT → (24,36) [g(24,33)] — now safe (the red is gone).
Hmm wait, do I even need to go right along row 24? The target is at (42,24) — to the left. After capturing both reds in row 24, I'm at (24,30). I need to get to (30,12) to capture red (36,12), then (36,18)→(42,18)→(42,24).
From (24,30): DOWN → (30,30) [g(27,30)] — moving DOWN, reds are gone from row 24… red (36,12) is far away. Safe.
9. DOWN → (30,30)
10. LEFT → (30,24)
11. LEFT → (30,18)
12. LEFT → (30,12) — moving LEFT, red (36,12) is directly below (30,12)! The move is horizontal, the red is below the destination — not on the line of the move → safe (E1 pattern: E1 was exactly this — the destination one hop from the red, the move not toward the red → safe).
13. DOWN → (36,12) [g(33,12)] — moving DOWN toward red (36,12), landing on top → capture.
14. RIGHT → (36,18) [g(36,15)] — safe (the red is gone).
15. DOWN → (42,18) [g(39,18)]
16. RIGHT → (42,24) [g(42,21)] — the target!
Total 16 moves.
Wait, can I shorten it? After step 7 (capturing red (24,30), at (24,30)), instead of going down at (24,30)… I have to go down at (24,30) (the only vertical bridge from row 24 to row 30, other than (24,48)→(30,48)). Actually g(27,48) also connects (24,48)-(30,48). From (24,30): RIGHT (24,36), RIGHT (24,42), RIGHT (24,48), DOWN (30,48), LEFT (30,42), LEFT (30,36), LEFT (30,30), LEFT (30,24), LEFT (30,18), LEFT (30,12) — longer. So going down at (24,30) is best.
Hmm, one more check on step 4: (30,36)→(30,30) LEFT. Red (24,30) is directly above the destination (30,30), one hop. The move is horizontal (not toward the red) → safe per E1. ✓ (E1: the destination (33,36) was one hop below the red (27,36), the move was RIGHT → safe.)
Step 5: (30,30)→(30,24) LEFT. Red (24,24) is above the destination, one hop. The move is horizontal → safe per E1. ✓
Step 6: (30,24)→(24,24) UP: landing on the red → capture per E2. ✓
Step 7: (24,24)→(24,30) RIGHT: landing on red (24,30) → capture. ✓
Step 9: (24,30)→(30,30) DOWN: moving DOWN. Any red one hop below (30,30)? None. Any red being moved toward? None. Safe.
Step 12: (30,18)→(30,12) LEFT: red (36,12) is below the destination, one hop. The move is horizontal → safe per E1. ✓
Step 13: (30,12)→(36,12) DOWN: landing on the red → capture. ✓
Step 16: (42,18)→(42,24) RIGHT: the target N is at (42,24). Landing on the target → level complete. ✓
Also check steps 1-3: no reds nearby. ✓
Now — the current state is GAME_OVER. The level will reset on the next action (as before). The board should reset to the initial level-3 layout (player (42,42), reds (24,24), (24,30), (36,12)). I should first take one action to trigger the reset, verify the board, then execute the plan. Actually, last time (after level 2's game over), the reset happened and I was able to act directly. Let me take the first action UP and check the state, then batch the rest.
Actually, to be safe: take UP (the first move of the plan) and verify the reset state (player at (36,42), reds in their initial positions). Then batch the remaining 15 moves.
Hmm, but if the reset hasn't happened yet (the board still shows the death frame with the red at (30,30)), the move might be invalid. Let me take UP and inspect.

grid = current_frame.ascii.split('\n')

import collections
cnt = collections.Counter()
for r in range(64):

print("state:", last_action_result.get('state'))
print("blue:", (min(x[0] for x in blue),min(x[1] for x in blue)) if blue else None)
print("red blocks:", [k for k in cnt if cnt[k]>3])
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
